T0A03: In US AC wiring, black = hot, white = neutral, green or bare = ground.

T0A06: All of these: three-wire cords, a common safety ground, and discharging high-voltage capacitors before working inside.
T0A07: Lightning arresters go on a grounded entry panel, where feed lines come into the building.
T0A08: A fuse or breaker goes in series with the hot wire only. Never the neutral.
T0A09: Bond all ground rods together with heavy wire or strap, so everything is at the same potential.
T0A10: Charging or discharging an unprotected battery too fast makes it overheat or out-gas (vent dangerous gas).
T0A11: Filter capacitors can hold a dangerous charge after the supply is switched off.
T0A12: Use a voltmeter and leads rated for the voltage you're measuring.
T0B01: Lightning wants a short, straight path. Keep ground connections short and direct, with no loops or sharp bends.
T0B02: All of these: training, staying tied off at all times, and an approved climbing harness.
T0B03: Never climb without a helper or observer.
T0B04: When putting up a tower, look for overhead power lines and stay well clear of them.
T0B05: A safety wire through a turnbuckle keeps vibration from unscrewing it.
T0B06: Place an antenna so that if it falls, no part can come within 10 feet of a power line.
T0B07: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it's fully retracted or has mechanical safety locks installed.
T0B08: Tower ground: a separate 8-foot ground rod at each leg, bonded to the tower and to each other.
T0B09: An antenna on a utility pole could touch high-voltage lines.
T0B10: Lightning grounding conductors: avoid sharp bends.
T0B11: Grounding requirements come from local electrical codes, not the FCC.
T0C01: Radio waves are non-ionizing radiation: not enough energy to break chemical bonds.
T0C02: Exposure limits are strictest from 30 to 300 MHz, where the body absorbs RF most. Of the choices, 50 MHz is in that range.
T0C03: Half the duty cycle = half the average exposure, so the allowed power density doubles (increases by a factor of 2).
T0C04: All of these affect exposure: frequency and power, distance, and the antenna's pattern.
T0C05: The body absorbs more RF at some frequencies than others, so the limits vary with frequency.
T0C06: All of these are acceptable: calculation from OET Bulletin 65, computer modeling, or calibrated field measurement.
T0C07: Touching an antenna while it transmits can give you an RF burn.
T0C08: To reduce exposure, move the antennas, since that's where the RF radiates from. Moving the transmitter doesn't help.
T0C09: Re-evaluate RF exposure whenever you change anything in the transmitter or antenna system.
T0C10: Duty cycle changes the average exposure, which is what the limits are based on.
T0C11: Duty cycle = the percentage of time the transmitter is actually transmitting.
T0C12: RF doesn't have enough energy to cause chemical changes or damage DNA. That's what makes it non-ionizing.
T0C13: The station licensee is responsible for keeping everyone under the RF exposure limits.
T1A01: Part of ham radio's stated purpose: advancing skills in the technical and communication sides of radio. It's a hobby for learning, not a public phone service.

T1A08: Repeater channels are recommended by a volunteer frequency coordinator recognized by local hams. No FCC involvement.

T1A10: To be a RACES control operator, you need certification of enrollment in a civil defense organization.
T1A11: Willful or malicious interference is prohibited. International VHF contacts and digital third-party traffic are fine.
T1B02: Any Technician or higher can work the ISS on VHF.
T1B03: 6 m runs 50-54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz is in it (a popular FM simplex frequency).
T1B04: 2 m runs 144-148 MHz. 146.52 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency.
T1B05: Technicians can use digital modes like FT8 on all three: 10, 6, and 2 m.
T1B07: CW-only segments: 50.0-50.1 MHz and 144.0-144.1 MHz, the bottom 100 kHz of 6 and 2 m.
T1B08: Where hams are secondary, primary users have priority. You must avoid interfering with them.
T1B09: All three reasons to stay off the exact band edge: display calibration error, sidebands spilling over, and drift.
T1B10: Above 50 MHz, SSB is allowed in at least part of every band.
T1B11: Technician HF power limit: 200 W PEP.
T1B12: Above 30 MHz, Technicians can run the full 1500 W PEP.
T1C01: New licenses today: Technician, General, Extra. Novice and Advanced are no longer issued.
T1C02: Any licensed amateur can apply for a vanity call sign.
T1C03: International contacts: only things incidental to amateur radio, plus personal remarks. No business.
T1C04: The FCC must be able to reach you by email. If it can't, your license can be revoked or suspended.
T1C05: Group D (Technician/General) format is 2 letters, a number, 3 letters: KF1XXX.
T1C06: On a US-documented vessel in international waters, you can operate with the master's permission.
T1C07: You can request renewal up to 90 days before your license expires.
T1C09: Grace period after expiration: 2 years to renew.
T1C10: Your first license: you can transmit once your grant appears in the FCC database, not when you leave the exam.
T1C11: An expired license means no transmitting, even in the grace period, until it's renewed.
T1D01: Contacts are banned only with countries that have notified the ITU they object.
T1D02: Broadcasting (sending to the general public) is prohibited. Code practice, event announcements, and telemetry are fine.
T1D03: Encoding to obscure meaning is allowed only for control commands to space stations or model craft.

T1D05: You can mention ham gear for sale or trade, as long as it's amateur equipment and not done regularly.
T1D06: Any indecent or obscene language is prohibited. There's no official word list.
T1D07: Auxiliary station example: the one-way link from a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter.
T1D08: Paid operation is allowed for teachers: when the communication is part of classroom instruction.
T1D09: You can support news gathering only for the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when no other means is available.
T1D10: Broadcasting = transmissions meant for the general public.
T1D11: Model craft control signals don't need ID. Everything else does.
T1D12: Test transmissions still need station ID.
T1E01: A station never transmits without a control operator. Even a repeater has one.
T1E02: Through a satellite, the control operator can be any ham allowed to transmit on the uplink frequency.
T1E03: The station licensee designates the control operator.
T1E04: Frequency privileges follow the control operator's license class.
T1E05: Control point = where the control operator actually performs the control function.
T1E06: A Technician can never control a station on Extra-only frequencies (except in an emergency).
T1E07: When the control operator isn't the licensee, both of them are responsible.
T1E09: Any station may be remotely controlled.
T1E10: Remote control example: running the station over the internet.
T1E11: Control operator: the ham the licensee designates as responsible for transmissions and rule compliance.
T1F01: An FCC representative can inspect the station and its records at any time, on request.
T1F02: Even with tactical calls, give your FCC call sign at least every 10 minutes and at the end.
T1F03: ID at least every 10 minutes during a contact, and at the end of it.
T1F04: Phone ID must be in English.
T1F05: Phone stations ID using CW or phone.
T1F06: All of these work on phone: stroke, slant, and slash all mean the / in a call sign.
T1F07: A non-licensed person can talk to a foreign station only if that country has a third-party agreement with the US.
T1F08: Third-party communication = a message passed between control operators on behalf of someone else.
T1F09: A repeater simultaneously retransmits a signal on another channel.
T1F10: If a repeater passes along a rule violation, the originating station's control operator is accountable.
T1F11: A club station license requires at least four members.
T2A01: 2 m repeater offset: plus or minus 600 kHz.
T2A02: The 2 m national FM simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz.
T2A03: 70 cm repeater offset: plus or minus 5 MHz.
T2A04: On a repeater: say their call sign, then yours. 'Break break' is for emergencies.

T2A10: A band plan is a voluntary guideline for which modes and activities go where in a band.
T2A11: Simplex = transmitting and receiving on the same frequency.

T2B02: CTCSS is a sub-audible tone sent with your voice to open a repeater's squelch.
T2B03: Linked repeaters: whatever one receives, all of them transmit.

T2B05: Audio dropping out on voice peaks on FM means you're talking too loudly (over-deviating).
T2B06: DTMF = two simultaneous tones (the telephone keypad).
T2B07: To join a DMR talkgroup, program its ID into your radio.
T2B08: If two stations interfere on the same frequency, they negotiate. Nobody owns a frequency.
T2B09: Simplex channels let nearby stations talk directly without tying up a repeater.
T2B10: QRM = interference from other stations (man-made). QRN = natural noise.

T2B13: Squelch mutes the receiver when no signal is present.
T2B14: A DMR talkgroup organizes traffic so you only hear the group you want.
T2C01: FCC rules always apply, even during RACES, ARES, or FEMA operations.
T2C02: Net control calls the net to order and directs the stations checking in.
T2C03: Spell unusual words with a standard phonetic alphabet.
T2C04: RACES is the FCC Part 97 service for civil defense communications in national emergencies.
T2C05: Traffic = formal messages passed through a net.
T2C06: ARES: licensed hams who voluntarily register their skills and equipment for public service.
T2C07: In a net, transmit only when net control directs you, unless you're reporting an emergency.
T2C08: Winlink relays email using call-sign-based email addresses.
T2C09: You can go outside your privileges only when there's an immediate threat to life or property.
T2C10: A message preamble holds the information needed to track the message.

T3A03: Long-distance VHF/UHF CW and SSB use horizontal polarization. FM and repeaters use vertical.

T3A12: Fog and rain have little effect on 10 m and 6 m. Weather only matters at microwave frequencies.
T3B01: A radio wave's electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other.
T3B02: Polarization = the orientation of the electric field.

T3B04: Radio waves travel at the speed of light. They are light, at a lower frequency.

T3B12: All radio frequencies travel at the same speed in free space.

T3C02: HF bounces off the ionosphere, so long-distance contacts are far more common on HF.
T3C03: Auroral signals sound distorted and raspy.

T3C07: Meteor scatter works best on 6 m.

T3C09: 10 m F-region DX: daytime (dawn to just after sunset), during high sunspot activity.

T9A10: A dipole radiates strongest broadside, at right angles to the wire.
T9A11: Antenna gain = a stronger signal in one direction compared with a reference antenna.
T9B01: Tape all of these outdoors: PL-259, BNC, and Type N. None of them are waterproof on their own.
T9B03: Coax is the most common feed line because it's easy to use and needs little special care when installing.
T9B04: An antenna tuner matches the antenna system's impedance to the rig's output.
T9B05: Coax loss increases at higher frequencies.
T9B06: Above 400 MHz, use Type N connectors.
T9B07: PL-259s are common at HF and VHF. They aren't waterproof and they aren't bayonet-type.
T9B08: All of these add coax loss: water, high SWR, and extra connectors.
T9B09: Erratic SWR = a loose connection somewhere.
T9B10: RG-213 is thicker than RG-58, with less loss.
T9B11: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss.
T9B12: SWR measures how well the load is matched to the feed line.
